finalResponse:
# The Future of Work: A Design Proposal for Global Endorsement and Local Adaptation

**Prepared for:** Executive Committee, with parallel circulation to Regional Leadership, Group Finance, Real Estate, IT, Legal & Tax, Group Security, and — where statutory bodies exist — to works councils and employee representatives *before* any external communication.

**Status:** Recommended design. All financial figures are illustrative placeholders pending validation by Group Finance and Real Estate; all statutory timelines require confirmation by local Legal counsel. Sections marked **[Requires consultation]** are not to be presented as decided in the affected jurisdictions.

---

## 1. Executive Summary

**The recommendation in three lines.** Stop asking how many days people should be in the office. Instead, (a) match work type to genuine co-location need, (b) push design decisions to the value-stream level within a deliberately thin global core, and (c) extend a comparable *flexibility investment per head* to desk-based and deskless populations alike — in different currencies, but at similar value.

**What it costs and what it returns (illustrative, to be validated).** For a company of ~60,000 people across ~40 countries, of whom roughly 40% are desk-based:

| Item | 3-year illustrative figure |
|---|---|
| Current annual property cost (rent, service charge, energy, FM) | €430m |
| Leases expiring or with break options within 36 months | ~34% of portfolio by cost |
| Net property saving from recommended portfolio scenario (regional hub-and-spoke) | €95–130m p.a. by year 3 |
| Reinvestment: fit-out quality, hub network, gathering travel, tooling, deskless amenity and scheduling systems | €55–70m p.a. |
| Home-working allowances and equipment (desk-based) | €18–24m p.a. |
| Manager and leader enablement (build + delivery) | €9m one-off, €3m p.a. |
| **Net structural saving retained** | **€25–45m p.a.** |

**Where the upside actually sits** — and this is the part that turns the programme from a cost exercise into a strategy one:

- **Hiring radius.** Access to 6–8 additional metropolitan labour markets per region without new legal entities, using the tiered mobility model in §10.
- **Offer acceptance and retention.** Flexibility is now a top-three factor in candidate decisions in most of our markets; a defensible, differentiated position is worth more than the property saving.
- **Follow-the-sun and resilience.** Distributed capability materially improves business continuity and reduces single-site concentration risk.
- **Carbon.** Commuting and portfolio reduction contribute measurably to stated Scope 1–3 targets; the offsetting increase in gathering travel must be counted honestly (see §5.4).

**What we ask of the Executive Committee.** Not approval of a rulebook — endorsement of seven principles, a governance body, a property scenario aligned to the lease calendar, and a set of stated positions on pay, mobility and stability. And, in Phase 0, a documented commitment from each Executive Committee member regarding their own working pattern. Nothing else in this document will survive if that step is skipped.

**A note on how we propose to proceed.** This design has been shaped by early listening across regions and, deliberately, has not been finalised. Several elements require formal consultation before they can be presented as decided. We would rather move a quarter more slowly and arrive with agreement intact than announce a scheme that quietly loses the confidence of colleagues and their representatives.

---

## 2. Seven Principles

**Principle 1 — Purpose over presence.**
Time and location are inputs; contribution is the output. Where they can be decoupled, decouple them. Where they genuinely cannot — production lines, laboratories, client sites, regulated environments, secure facilities — the constraint is stated with its reason, and Principle 7 applies instead.

**Principle 2 — A thin centre, thick edges.**
The centre owns only what must be common: legal and tax compliance, security, equity measurement, the tooling backbone, and a short list of non-negotiables. Rhythms, meeting norms, office use and rituals belong closer to the work. A short list of global rules is easier to respect than a long one.

**Principle 3 — The value stream is the unit of design.**
Friction lives in the interfaces between people, not in individuals working alone. Working agreements are therefore authored at the level of interdependency — the value stream, product line or service chain — not the org chart box (§6).

**Principle 4 — Flexibility must be equitably distributed, and measured.**
Flexibility that flows to the senior, the confident, the geographically central or the well-housed is a privilege, not a benefit. We assume proximity bias and time-zone burden exist until measurement shows otherwise.

**Principle 5 — Local adaptation is a feature, not a compliance failure.**
Divergence between Singapore, Munich and Monterrey is evidence the framework is working. What must be consistent is the fairness of outcomes, not the shape of arrangements.

**Principle 6 — Learn openly, but do not destabilise lives.**
Arrangements carry review dates; individuals carry stability guarantees (§12.3). Reversibility at the system level is paired with notice periods at the personal level, because colleagues make housing, schooling and eldercare decisions on the strength of what we tell them.

**Principle 7 — Flexibility for all, in different currencies.**
Every colleague receives a flexibility investment; its form differs by role. For deskless colleagues that means predictability, control over time, and quality of the on-site day. The commitment is that **flexibility investment per head is broadly comparable across populations**, and reported as such. This principle exists to prevent the outcome we consider the single largest risk in the programme: a two-tier culture in which one population receives autonomy and the other receives an explanation.

---

## 3. Two Populations, One Commitment

Roughly 60% of our colleagues cannot choose their location. A framework that speaks only to the other 40% would damage cohesion in exactly the places where cohesion is hardest won — plants, depots, contact centres, retail and field service.

**The deskless flexibility package (recommended standard):**

| Element | Commitment |
|---|---|
| Schedule notice | Rosters published ≥ 3 weeks ahead; no unilateral change inside 7 days without premium |
| Shift swapping | Self-service, peer-to-peer, manager-approved by exception only |
| Compressed and split patterns | Available where safety and coverage permit; requests answered within 10 working days with a reason |
| Banked time / time-account | Accrual and withdrawal within statutory limits, portable across the year |
| Part-remote elements of deskless roles | Training, admin, planning, debriefs shifted off-site where feasible — typically 5–15% of hours |
| On-site quality | Quiet rooms, decent break space, lockers, connectivity, parking/transport support, heating and cooling |
| Voice | Frontline representation on the Work Design Council; site-level design volunteers |
| Career access | Remote-accessible training and internal mobility; no advancement path that requires relocation without support |

**Reporting.** The equity scorecard (§11) reports flexibility investment per head, request-approval rates, and schedule-stability performance separately for deskless and desk-based populations. Where a gap opens, it is a Council agenda item, not a footnote.

**[Requires consultation]** In unionised sites, scheduling and time-account provisions are subject to collective bargaining. We recommend approaching representatives with the *principle* and a genuine blank on the mechanism, rather than a finished scheme.

---

## 4. Architecture and Governance

### 4.1 The four layers

| Layer | Owns | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Global core** (minimal) | Non-negotiables | Employment/tax compliance, security standards, pay and promotion equity, tooling backbone, measurement, ethical floor (accessibility, rest and disconnection with the on-call carve-out in §8.4) |
| **Region / country** | Legal and cultural translation | Statutory consultation, labour law, office portfolio, allowances calibrated to local cost and housing, holiday and time-zone conventions |
| **Value stream / team** | The real design work | Working agreement: overlap band, meeting-free blocks, async defaults, in-person cadence and purpose, decision rights, response norms |
| **Individual** | Personal fit | Where and when within the agreement, workspace, negotiated exceptions (caregiving, health, accessibility, visa) |

An outer layer may constrain an inner one, but must record why. Operationally: the constraint is logged in the Work Design Register with a named owner, a category (legal / security / customer coverage / cost / safety), and a review date. Unrecorded constraints lapse at the next quarterly review. Appeals go to the Council, which answers within 15 working days.

### 4.2 Governance

**Work Design Council.** Chaired by the Chief People Officer; sponsored by the COO as named Executive owner. Members: HR, Real Estate & Workplace, IT, Legal & Tax, Group Security, Finance, plus **six rotating seats** — three regional representatives and three non-managerial colleagues (at least one deskless). Quarterly, with a monthly working group.

**Decision rights (summary RACI):**

| Decision | Accountable | Consulted |
|---|---|---|
| Global non-negotiables; ethical floor | Executive Committee | Council; employee representatives |
| Portfolio scenario, capital, lease action | Real Estate, with CFO | Region; Council |
| Country policy translation; allowances | Regional HR lead | Legal; works council; Finance |
| Working agreements; in-person cadence | Value-stream leader | Interdependent teams; team members |
| Individual arrangements | Line manager | HR partner where an exception applies |
| Cross-border remote requests | Global Mobility | Tax, Legal, Security |
| Exceptions and appeals | Work Design Council | Requesting party |

**Service levels.** Individual arrangement requests: answered in 10 working days. Cross-border requests: 20. Escalated inter-team conflicts: resolved by the shared leader within 5 working days, or referred upward automatically. Silence is not an answer; unanswered requests default to "granted provisionally, pending review."

---

## 5. Property Portfolio and the Financial Case

### 5.1 The lease calendar is the forcing function

Property decisions run on a multi-year clock that will not wait for pilot results. We therefore recommend sequencing decisions by expiry, not by programme phase:

| Horizon | Portfolio share (illustrative) | Recommended posture |
|---|---|---|
| 0–12 months | 11% by cost | Decide now on scenario logic; prefer short extensions to preserve optionality |
| 12–36 months | 23% | Decide by end of Design phase; pilots inform fit-out, not footprint |
| 36 months+ | 66% | Decide after pilots; use the interval to improve occupancy data |

### 5.2 Scenarios

| Scenario | Footprint change | Annual cost effect | Capacity | Principal risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Hold** | 0% | – | 100% | Pays for empty space; signals no change |
| **B. Consolidate to fewer, larger sites** | –25% | –€105m | 70% at 1:1.4 sharing | Longer commutes; concentration risk; poorest fit with local housing realities |
| **C. Regional hub-and-spoke** *(recommended)* | –22% desk area, +14 small hubs | –€95m gross, –€60m net of hub cost and fit-out | 85% at 1:1.6 | Operational complexity; requires disciplined booking data |
| **D. Radical distributed** | –45% | –€180m | 45% | High attrition risk in offices that function as social and mentorship centres; hard to reverse |

We recommend **C**, on grounds of reversibility and reduced disruption to established site communities. D produces the larger number and, in our assessment, the larger cultural cost — and it is the hardest to unwind if we are wrong.

### 5.3 Reinvestment thesis

We recommend committing, publicly, that **55–65% of gross property savings are reinvested** rather than banked: fit-out quality in retained sites, the hub network, gathering travel budgets held at team level, deskless amenity and scheduling technology, tooling, and manager enablement. A programme that visibly returns value to colleagues will be met very differently from one that appears to be a cost exercise wearing the language of flexibility.

### 5.4 Costs that are routinely underestimated

- **Gathering travel.** Organisations typically under-forecast this by 2–3×. Budget €900–1,400 per person per gathering, all-in, and hold the budget at value-stream level with a carbon allocation attached.
- **Allowances and equipment.** Statutory in several jurisdictions (e.g. remote-work allowance obligations, home-workspace duties). Model at €300–650 per desk-based head per year, calibrated locally.
- **Tooling duplication** during transition; **hub and co-working access fees**; **occupancy analytics**; **dilapidations and exit costs** on vacated leases.

---

## 6. Working Agreements: Defaults, Not Blank Pages

Handing thousands of teams a blank page produces uneven quality and consumes manager time we have not budgeted. We therefore recommend **opinionated defaults** that a team can adopt in ten minutes, and deviate from with a one-paragraph written rationale.

### 6.1 Published defaults

| Element | Default | Deviation |
|---|---|---|
| Core overlap | 3 hours per working day across the value stream, rotated (§8.5) | Written rationale; must not push the burden onto one region |
| Meeting-free block | One half-day per week, common across the value stream | Value-stream leader approval |
| In-person cadence | Distributed teams: 4 days per quarter, purpose-stated. Co-located teams: 2 days per week anchor. Hybrid mixed: 1 anchor day per week plus quarterly gathering | Team may increase freely; reduction needs rationale |
| Channel semantics | Chat = today; email = 2 working days; ticket = per SLA; call = decisions, disagreement, relationships | Local adaptation encouraged |
| Meeting hygiene | No status meetings; written pre-read; decisions logged | None |
| Inclusion rule | If one participant is remote, all join individually | None — this is a global non-negotiable |
| Review | Quarterly, 45 minutes | None |

### 6.2 Interface protocol (the incompatibility problem)

1. Agreements are authored at the **value stream**, not the team. Teams may add, not contradict.
2. Where two interdependent groups conflict, the **more distributed party's constraints take precedence**, because their options are fewer.
3. Conflict is raised in writing to the shared leader; resolution within **5 working days**; outcome recorded in the Register.
4. Unresolved conflicts escalate automatically. No one has to force a confrontation to get a decision — the clock does it, which preserves working relationships between the parties.
5. Each value stream nominates a **working-agreement steward** (not necessarily the manager) who holds the document and convenes the review.

### 6.3 What the agreement covers

Overlap and protected focus time; default channel per work type; what earns synchronous time; response norms and the meaning of silence; the specific purposes of coming together (kickoffs, conflict resolution, design bursts, onboarding, celebration) and the cadence those imply; decision rights; the inclusion check. One to two pages, visible company-wide. The value lies as much in the conversation as in the document.

---
